title: Which statements about a number and its digit sum are correct?
description: Four statements link a number with the sum of its digits. The video tests them with seven thousand three hundred nine and four thousand five hundred eighty one. Keeko's doubt is that only the first two statements are correct, because the last two use the word not.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by nine, so they are divisible by nine together or not at all. Watch for students who accept the statements about divisible numbers but doubt the ones about numbers that are not divisible.

source: Test the four statements with 7309 and 4581, then decide whi
video_script.why: The student can find a remainder on division by nine from the digit sum and now uses this to judge four statements about divisibility by nine.
video_script.substitution: Find the digit sum of each number, compare the remainders of the number and its digit sum, and read off each statement.
video_script.anchor: dots in groups of nine, a number and its digit sum each shown as whole groups of nine with the same dots left over
video_script.wrong_answer: only the first two are correct
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko trusts the statements about divisible numbers and doubts the ones that say not divisible, although the same remainder rule covers both.
maths_rules: 7309: digit sum 7 + 3 + 0 + 9 = 19 = 2 x 9 + 1, and 7309 = 9 x 812 + 1; both leave remainder 1, neither is divisible by 9
4581: digit sum 4 + 5 + 8 + 1 = 18 = 2 x 9, and 4581 = 9 x 509; both leave remainder 0, both are divisible by 9
every place value leaves remainder 1 on division by 9, so a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder
same remainder means both are divisible by 9 or neither is
if divisible by 9 then the digit sum is divisible by 9, and the other way round
if not divisible by 9 then the digit sum is not divisible by 9, and the other way round
video_script.design: Two numbers, each beside its digit sum, shown as groups of nine with the leftover dots. The same leftover appears for the number and its digit sum, and the four statements are then read off.
